items.question: Group 1 is 2, 6 and 9, and group 2 is 4, 7 and 10 (practice values). Make both groups add up to the same sum with one swap.
steps: The gap is 21 − 17 = 4. Half of the gap is 4 ÷ 2 = 2.
Look for a number of group 1 and a number of group 2 that differ by 2. The numbers 2 and 4 differ by 2, because 4 − 2 = 2.
Swap the 2 and the 4. Group 1 is now 4, 6 and 9, and 4 + 6 + 9 = 19. Group 2 is now 2, 7 and 10, and 2 + 7 + 10 = 19.
A swap that does not work: swap 6 and 7. They differ by 1, so group 1 becomes 18 and group 2 becomes 20, and the gap is still 2.
Check: group 1 went up by 2 and group 2 went down by 2, so the gap closed by 2 + 2 = 4.
items.answer: Swap the 2 and the 4: both groups add up to 19

source: Making Sums Equal: puzzle (a)

items.question: In each of the following, there are two groups of numbers. Look carefully at the numbers in each group and their sums. Interchange pairs of numbers between the two groups to make their sums equal. Try to do this using the least number of moves. (a): Group 1: 1, 2, 7, 9 (sum 19). Group 2: 3, 4, 5, 9 (sum 21).
steps: Group 1: 1 + 2 + 7 + 9 = 19. Group 2: 3 + 4 + 5 + 9 = 21. The gap is 21 − 19 = 2, and half of the gap is 1.
The hint swaps 2 and 5. Then group 1 is 1 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 22 and group 2 is 3 + 4 + 2 + 9 = 18. The gap grows to 4, so that swap is not the one.
We need a number of group 1 and a number of group 2 that differ by 1. Only 2 and 3 differ by 1.
Swap 2 and 3. Group 1 is now 1, 3, 7 and 9, and 1 + 3 + 7 + 9 = 20. Group 2 is now 2, 4, 5 and 9, and 2 + 4 + 5 + 9 = 20.
The sums were not equal to begin with, so one move is the fewest. Check: both sums are 20.
items.answer: Swap 2 and 3: both groups add up to 20. This takes 1 move.

source: Making Sums Equal: puzzle (b)

items.question: In each of the following, there are two groups of numbers. Look carefully at the numbers in each group and their sums. steps: Group 1: 5 + 7 + 12 + 15 = 39. Group 2: 9 + 11 + 13 + 14 = 47. The gap is 47 − 39 = 8, and half of the gap is 4.
We need a number of group 1 and a number of group 2 that differ by 4. The pairs 5 and 9, and 7 and 11, both differ by 4.
Swap 5 and 9. Group 1 is now 9, 7, 12 and 15, and 9 + 7 + 12 + 15 = 43. Group 2 is now 5, 11, 13 and 14, and 5 + 11 + 13 + 14 = 43.
The other pair works too: swapping 7 and 11 gives 5 + 11 + 12 + 15 = 43 and 9 + 7 + 13 + 14 = 43.
One move is the fewest. Check: both sums are 43.

source: Making Sums Equal: puzzle (c)

items.question: In each of the following, there are two groups of numbers. Look carefully at the numbers in each group and their sums. Interchange pairs of numbers between the two groups to make their sums equal. Try to do this using the least number of moves. (c): Group 1: 11, 15, 19, 23 (sum 68). Group 2: 13, 17, 21, 25 (sum 76).
steps: Group 1: 11 + 15 + 19 + 23 = 68. Group 2: 13 + 17 + 21 + 25 = 76. The gap is 76 − 68 = 8, and half of the gap is 4.

One swap needs two numbers that differ by 4. The pairs that differ by 2 are 11 and 13, 15 and 17, 19 and 21, and 23 and 25. Every other pair differs by 6 or more. No pair differs by 4, so one swap is not enough.
Use two swaps that each differ by 2. Together they close the gap: 2 + 2 = 4, which is half of the gap.
Swap 11 and 13, and swap 15 and 17. Group 1 is now 13, 17, 19 and 23, and 13 + 17 + 19 + 23 = 72. Group 2 is now 11, 15, 21 and 25, and 11 + 15 + 21 + 25 = 72.
Two moves are the fewest. Check: both sums are 72.

items.question: In each of the following, there are two groups of numbers. Look carefully at the numbers in each group and their sums. Interchange pairs of numbers between the two groups to make their sums equal. Try to do this using the least number of moves. (d): Group 1: 77, 78, 79, 80 (sum 314). Group 2: 81, 82, 83, 84 (sum 330).
steps: Group 1: 77 + 78 + 79 + 80 = 314. Group 2: 81 + 82 + 83 + 84 = 330. The gap is 330 − 314 = 16, and half of the gap is 8.
The biggest difference between a number of group 1 and a number of group 2 is 84 − 77 = 7. That is less than 8, so one swap is not enough.
Use two swaps whose differences add up to 8. Two swaps that each differ by 4 do it: 4 + 4 = 8.

Swap 77 and 81, which differ by 81 − 77 = 4, and swap 78 and 82, which differ by 82 − 78 = 4. Group 1 is now 81, 82, 79 and 80, and 81 + 82 + 79 + 80 = 322. Group 2 is now 77, 78, 83 and 84, and 77 + 78 + 83 + 84 = 322.
Two moves are the fewest. Check: both sums are 322.

source: Relationship Between Addition and Subtraction: fill the blanks

items.question: Find the relationship between the numbers in the given statements and fill in the blanks appropriately. (a): If 46 + 21 = 67, then, 67 − 21 = ___. 67 − 46 = ___. (b): If 198 − 98 = 100, then, 100 + ___ = 198. 198 − ___ = 98. (c): If 189 + 98 = 287, then, 287 − 98 = ___. 287 − 189 = ___. (d): If 872 − 672 = 200, then, 200 + ___ = 872. 872 − ___ = 672.
steps: (a): In 46 + 21 = 67 the whole is 67. Take a part away: 67 − 21 = 46 and 67 − 46 = 21.
(b): In 198 − 98 = 100 the whole is 198 and the parts are 98 and 100. The parts added make the whole: 100 + 98 = 198. The whole minus a part: 198 − 100 = 98.
(c): In 189 + 98 = 287 the whole is 287. Take a part away: 287 − 98 = 189 and 287 − 189 = 98.
(d): In 872 − 672 = 200 the whole is 872 and the parts are 672 and 200. The parts added make the whole: 200 + 672 = 872. The whole minus a part: 872 − 200 = 672.
Check (a): 46 + 21 = 67 is true.

source: Sums of Consecutive Numbers: even or odd

items.question: In each of the boxes above, state whether the sums are even or odd. Explain why this is happening.
steps: Box 1 (2 consecutive numbers): the sums 3, 5, 7 and 9 are all odd.
Why: two consecutive numbers are one even number and one odd number, and even plus odd is odd.
Box 2 (3 consecutive numbers): the sums 6, 9, 12 and 15 are even, odd, even, odd.
Why: the sum is 3 times the middle number, so it is odd when the middle number is odd and even when the middle number is even. The middle numbers 2, 3, 4 and 5 take turns, even and odd.
Box 3 (4 consecutive numbers): the sums 10, 14, 18 and 22 are all even.
Why: 4 consecutive numbers make two pairs of consecutive numbers. Each pair adds to an odd number, and odd plus odd is even.
Check: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 is even.
items.answer: Box 1: all odd, one even and one odd number. Box 2: even and odd in turn, 3 times the middle number. Box 3: all even, two odd pairs.

source: Let Us Solve (adding large numbers): the six sums

items.question: Find the following sums. Try not to write ten thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens and ones at the top. Just align the digits properly, at least for the smaller numbers. (a): 238 + 367; (b): 1,234 + 12,345; (c): 12 + 123; (d): 46,120 + 12,890; (e): 878 + 8,789; (f): 1,749 + 17,490.
steps: (a): Align the ones: 238 + 367. Ones: 8 + 7 = 15, write 5 and regroup. Tens: 3 + 6 + 1 = 10, write 0 and regroup. Hundreds: 2 + 3 + 1 = 6. So 238 + 367 = 605.
(b): Align the ones: 1,234 + 12,345. Ones: 4 + 5 = 9. Tens: 3 + 4 = 7. Hundreds: 2 + 3 = 5. Thousands: 1 + 2 = 3. Ten thousands: 0 + 1 = 1. So the sum is 13,579.
(c): 12 + 123: the 2 of 12 goes under the 3 of 123 and the 1 of 12 under the 2. Ones: 2 + 3 = 5. Tens: 1 + 2 = 3. Hundreds: 1. So the sum is 135.
(d): 46,120 + 12,890. Ones: 0 + 0 = 0. Tens: 2 + 9 = 11, write 1 and regroup. Hundreds: 1 + 8 + 1 = 10, write 0 and regroup. Thousands: 6 + 2 + 1 = 9. Ten thousands: 4 + 1 = 5. So the sum is 59,010.
(e): 878 + 8,789. Ones: 8 + 9 = 17, write 7 and regroup. Tens: 7 + 8 + 1 = 16, write 6 and regroup. Hundreds: 8 + 7 + 1 = 16, write 6 and regroup. Thousands: 8 + 1 = 9. So the sum is 9,667.
(f): 1,749 + 17,490. Ones: 9 + 0 = 9. Tens: 4 + 9 = 13, write 3 and regroup. Hundreds: 7 + 4 + 1 = 12, write 2 and regroup. Thousands: 1 + 7 + 1 = 9. Ten thousands: 0 + 1 = 1. So the sum is 19,239.

source: Example 5: The ship from Mumbai to Chennai

items.question: The total distance of the sea route from Mumbai to Chennai is 2,700 km. A ship starting from Mumbai first reaches the Cochin port, travelling 1,083 km by sea. How much more distance does it have to travel to reach the Chennai port?

(e): 56 + 56,789: align the ones. Ones: 6 + 9 = 15, write 5 and regroup. Tens: 5 + 8 + 1 = 14, write 4 and regroup. Hundreds: 7 + 1 = 8. The thousands 6 and the ten thousands 5 come down. So the sum is 56,845.

items.question: Part A: A traveller starts a trip with ₹15,000. She spends ₹4,250 on fuel, is paid back ₹2,000 by a friend, then spends ₹3,160 on tickets. How much money is left? Part B: A school council has ₹50,000 and wants to buy things that cost ₹19,820, ₹14,480 and ₹9,765. Estimate whether the money is enough, then check (practice values).
steps: Part A. Start with 15,000 rupees.
She spends 4,250 rupees, so take away: 15,000 − 4,250 = 10,750.
She is paid back 2,000 rupees, so add: 10,750 + 2,000 = 12,750.
She spends 3,160 rupees on tickets, so take away: 12,750 − 3,160 = 9,590.
She is left with ₹9,590.
Part B. Round each price up to the next thousand: 19,820 becomes 20,000, 14,480 becomes 15,000 and 9,765 becomes 10,000.
The real prices are less than the rounded prices, so the real total is less than 45,000, and 45,000 is less than 50,000. The estimate says: enough.
Check with the real prices: 19,820 + 14,480 = 34,300.
50,000 − 44,065 = 5,935 is left, so the money is enough.

items.question: Will this method work if the units digit is 0? What do you think? What other methods can you use to find the missing number to fill in the blanks? Share your thoughts in the class. (a): 180 + ___ = 1,000; (b): 760 + ___ = 1,000; (c): 400 + ___ = 1,000.
steps: (a): 180: 1 needs 8, 8 needs 1 and 0 needs 9 to make 9. So 180 + 819 = 999, and the blank is 819 + 1 = 820.
(b): 760: 7 needs 2, 6 needs 3 and 0 needs 9. So 760 + 239 = 999, and the blank is 239 + 1 = 240.
(c): 400: 4 needs 5, 0 needs 9 and 0 needs 9. So 400 + 599 = 999, and the blank is 599 + 1 = 600.
Yes, the method works when the units digit is 0. The last nine is 9, and adding 1 makes it carry.
Another method: count up to the next hundred and then to 1,000. For 180: 180 + 20 = 200, then 200 + 800 = 1,000, so the blank is 20 + 800 = 820.

items.question: Jincy opened her piggy bank. She found 8 coins of ₹1, 9 coins of ₹2 and 5 coins of ₹5. She wants to buy stickers worth ₹38. What possible combination of coins can she use to pay the exact amount?
steps: All the coins together make 8 + 18 + 25 = 51 rupees: 8 coins of ₹1 make ₹8, 9 coins of ₹2 make ₹18 and 5 coins of ₹5 make ₹25. So ₹38 can be paid.
Go through the number of ₹5 coins, from the most (5) to the fewest, and fill the rest with ₹2 and ₹1 coins.

5 coins of ₹5 make ₹25, and ₹13 more is needed: 6 coins of ₹2 and 1 coin of ₹1, or 5 coins of ₹2 and 3 coins of ₹1, or 4 coins of ₹2 and 5 coins of ₹1, or 3 coins of ₹2 and 7 coins of ₹1. That is 4 ways.

4 coins of ₹5 make ₹20, and ₹18 more is needed: 9 coins of ₹2, or 8 coins of ₹2 and 2 coins of ₹1, or 7 coins of ₹2 and 4 coins of ₹1, or 6 coins of ₹2 and 6 coins of ₹1, or 5 coins of ₹2 and 8 coins of ₹1. That is 5 ways.
3 coins of ₹5 make ₹15, and ₹23 more is needed: 9 coins of ₹2 and 5 coins of ₹1, or 8 coins of ₹2 and 7 coins of ₹1. That is 2 ways.
With 2 coins of ₹5, which make ₹10, ₹28 more is needed, but all the ₹2 and ₹1 coins make only 18 + 8 = 26 rupees. So it cannot be done, and fewer ₹5 coins is even less possible.
In all there are 4 + 5 + 2 = 11 combinations.

items.question: Part A: A table shows three buses. Bus A travelled 4,215 km and was bought in 2015, Bus B travelled 6,380 km and was bought in 2018, and Bus C travelled 5,094 km and was bought in 2021. Which bus travelled the most? What is the difference between the most and the least, and between Bus B and Bus C? A driver was 25 years old when Bus C was bought. In which year was the driver born? Part B: 12,450 tickets were printed for a fair and 12,615 people came. Were the tickets enough, and how many were short or extra? On another day 9,830 tickets were printed and 9,415 people came (practice values).
steps: Part A. Compare the distances: 6,380 is the most, so Bus B travelled the most. 4,215 is the least, so Bus A travelled the least.
The difference between the most and the least is 6,380 − 4,215 = 2,165 km.
The difference between Bus B and Bus C is 6,380 − 5,094 = 1,286 km.
Bus C was bought in 2021 and the driver was 25 then, so the driver was born in 2021 − 25 = 1996.
Part B. Compare 12,450 and 12,615. 12,450 is less than 12,615, so the tickets were not enough.
The number short is 12,615 − 12,450 = 165.
Compare 9,830 and 9,415. 9,830 is more than 9,415, so the tickets were enough.
The number extra is 9,830 − 9,415 = 415.
items.answer: Part A: Bus B travelled the most; 2,165 km; 1,286 km; the driver was born in 1996. Part B: first day: not enough, 165 short; second day: enough, 415 extra
